vignette:
He is seventy-five now, a widowed Middle Eastern man who has spent most of his life shaping stone and metal with his hands. Before the accident, his days are organized by the steady rituals of a sculptor: early coffee, a slow walk through the studio, fingers brushing over unfinished surfaces as if greeting old friends. He likes heavy materials, likes the argument between force and patience. He says that when he works well, he can feel time disappear. After his wife dies several years earlier, the studio becomes not only his livelihood but also his refuge, the place where grief can be given weight and contour.

The accident happens on an ordinary afternoon. He is alone in the studio, moving a large block with a hoist he has used many times before. He notices a frayed section of cable and thinks, briefly, that he will replace it tomorrow. Then everything happens at once. There is a sharp metallic crack, the scream of the hoist giving way, and the stone swings violently toward him. He jumps, but not far enough. It catches his leg and knocks him to the floor, pinning him awkwardly beneath part of its weight. He cannot breathe for a moment. Dust fills his mouth. The room that has always felt like sanctuary becomes a trap of shattered plaster, twisted metal, and impossible pressure.

What stays with him most is not the pain but the certainty, in those minutes, that he is about to die alone. He can hear his own voice calling out, thin and unfamiliar. He remembers trying to free himself and feeling the hot surge of panic when the stone does not move. He thinks of his wife then, absurdly clearly, imagining her finding out after the fact. By the time a neighboring artisan hears him and calls for help, he is shaking so hard he can barely answer questions. In the hospital, he survives with fractures, bruising, and months of rehabilitation. People tell him he is lucky. He nods because that is what is expected.

When he first returns home, he tells himself the worst is over. Instead, his world begins to narrow. Sleep becomes a place of ambush. He wakes drenched in sweat, hearing again the cable snap, feeling the crush of weight on his leg, the helplessness in his chest. Sometimes in the seconds after waking he does not know where he is; he reaches for the side of the bed where his wife used to sleep and feels only empty sheets, and the loneliness of that realization lands fresh each time. During the day, sudden metallic noises-a dropped pan, a truck hitting a pothole, the rattle of a chain-link gate-send a jolt through him so strong that his heart pounds and his hands tremble. He hates that his body reacts before his mind can catch up.

He tries to go back to the studio. At first he stands outside with the key in his hand, unable to make himself unlock the door. When he does step inside, the smell of stone dust turns his stomach. His eyes go immediately to the repaired hoist. He knows, rationally, that it has been replaced and inspected, but his body does not believe in rationality anymore. He feels exposed, as if the room itself is watching him. He begins working only on very small pieces near the entrance, keeping the door open, never staying long. Projects that once would have taken a week stretch across months. He avoids commissions involving heavy stone and tells clients, with irritation he cannot hide, that he prefers bronze now.

His family notices he is not the same, though he offers them little. His adult children call and visit, but he waves away questions. In the culture he comes from, he is used to being the sturdy one, the father, the man who endures. He feels ashamed by how frightened he has become. When relatives praise his survival, he becomes quiet or leaves the room. He cannot bear being told it is "in the past," because for him it is not past at all; it returns in images, in sensations, in the split second before sleep. He has begun to avoid gatherings because the noise exhausts him and because he cannot follow conversations without scanning the room for exits, hazards, anything suspended overhead.

He is more irritable than he used to be. Small frustrations-a late delivery, a misplaced chisel, a neighbor's barking dog-can bring a flash of anger that surprises him. Just as often, he feels nothing where he expects feeling to be. He sits for long stretches in the studio staring at a half-finished figure, unable to imagine what comes next. Sculpture had always been the way he metabolizes experience; now even his art feels altered. The forms he makes have become narrower, enclosed, compressed. He says he used to carve bodies in motion, turning outward. Now, without planning to, he keeps making figures folded inward, arms drawn across the chest.

He speaks of the accident as if it divided his life into before and after. Before, he trusted his hands, his materials, his space. After, he moves through the world as though danger has become intimate and ordinary. Even on calm days, part of him remains braced. He misses the man who could lose himself in work. What troubles him most is not only that he nearly died, but that he no longer fully feels alive in the place that once gave his life shape.
